On a 100M-vector benchmark, NemoANN reduces SSD reads by about 10x and improves throughput by 8.0x over post-filtering and by 5.0x over PipeANN-Filter, a state-of-the-art filtered SSD system, at 10% selectivity and 90% recall. The gains over post-filtering grow at lower selectivity, reaching 13.1x at 5% selectivity.

papers.title: LZn : Robust LoRa Frame Synchronization Under Frame Collisions and Ultra-Low SNR Conditions
papers.summary: LoRa has become a widely adopted wireless modulation scheme in LPWANs due to its low cost, long range, and minimal transmission power. However, collisions between frames of the same spreading factor -- common in dense LoRa deployments -- prevent conventional LoRa receivers from detecting and correctly decoding frames. Recent work has introduced methods to improve recovery, yet their detection stage degrades sharply under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and high collision rates. In this work, we introduce LZn, a synchronization scheme driven by a minimum-based spectral intersection across consecutive symbols. While preamble search incurs a modest overhead, LZn reduces the cost of fine synchronization by two to three orders of magnitude compared to existing collision-tolerant receivers. Our method enables robust frame synchronization even under multiple packet overlaps or extremely low SNR conditions. We evaluate LZn on simulations and three independent, real-world LoRa datasets. LZn improves detection sensitivity by up to 10 dB and increases detection probability by up to 1.54x. In real-world datasets, LZn improves decoding by 3.46x in the most challenging single-user scenario and up to 1.22x in collision scenarios compared to the second best collision-tolerant scheme (TnB). These results demonstrate that LZn substantially improves the frame recovery of LoRa receivers, while remaining compatible with real-time requirements.

papers.title: DeGenTWeb: A First Look at MGT-dominant Websites
papers.summary: Many news reports have claimed that machine-generated text (MGT) from large language models (LLMs) is taking over the web. However, these claims are typically not based on a representative sample of the web, and the methodology underlying them is often opaque. Consequently, we lack an understanding of the true prevalence and characteristics of MGT on the web. We describe DeGenTWeb, which systematically identifies MGT-dominant websites: sites whose informational prose content is mostly MGT, with little human input. We show how to adapt detectors of MGT for use on web pages, and how to aggregate detection results from multiple pages on a site for accurate site-level categorization. DeGenTWeb mislabels only 0.12% of human-authored sites as MGT-dominant. We find that 20.9% of the sites archived by Common Crawl between January and July 2026 and 13.6% of the sites linked from Bing's search results in 2025 are MGT-dominant. These figures are lower bounds on the prevalence of MGT-dominant sites. We also find that the fraction of MGT-dominant sites is growing over time, and that many such sites share the same owner. We will release all of our code and data after publication.

papers.title: SplitZip: Ultra Fast Lossless KV Compression for Disaggregated LLM Serving
papers.summary: Contemporary systems serving large language models (LLMs) have adopted prefill-decode disaggregation to load-balance between the compute-bound prefill phase and the memory-bound decode phase. Under this design, prefill workers generate a KV cache that must be transferred to decode workers before generation can begin. With these workers residing on different physical systems, this transfer becomes a significant bottleneck to serving LLMs at scale, especially for long-input and agentic workloads. Existing lossless codecs are unsuitable here as they primarily target offline weight compression, run on CPUs, or use variable-length coding whose compression cannot keep up with KV production during prefill. We introduce SplitZip, a GPU-friendly lossless compressor for KV cache transfer that preserves KV tensors bitwise and integrates into existing serving frameworks without modifying model execution. SplitZip exploits redundancy in floating-point exponents of KV activations, encoding frequent exponent values with fixed-length codes and routing rare exponents through a sparse escape stream of (position, value). A calibrated top-16 exponent codebook eliminates online histogramming, while the regular dense path and sparse escape correction make both encoding and decoding efficient on GPUs. On real BF16 activation tensors, SplitZip achieves $613.3$ GB/s compression throughput and $2181.8$ GB/s decompression throughput, outperforming prior lossless compressors on the critical codec path. End-to-end transfer experiments show up to $1.32\times$ speedup for BF16 KV cache transfer, $1.30\times$ speedup for TTFT, and $1.23\times$ increase in Request Throughput. The same approach extends to FP8 KV caches, providing up to $1.14\times$ compression over native E5M2. Code is available at https://github.com/Intelligent-Microsystems-Lab/SplitZip

papers.title: Reward-Weighted On-Policy Distillation with an Open Property-Equivalence Verifier for NL-to-SVA Generation
papers.summary: Specialized language models for translating natural language (NL) into SystemVerilog assertions (SVA) reach approximately 76\% accuracy on NL2SVA-Human, but aggregate scores obscure errors on bounded-delay and liveness specifications. Models often reuse a small set of implication templates where different temporal behavior is required. Supervised fine-tuning rewards agreement with reference tokens, whereas SVA correctness depends on property equivalence. We propose \emph{reward-weighted on-policy distillation} (RWOPD), which uses an open SymbiYosys+Z3 property-equivalence checker to select student rollouts and weight their distillation loss. A frozen 14B teacher supplies forward Kullback--Leibler (KL) supervision at each response token; equivalent rollouts receive greater weight than one-sided implications. Starting from curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), RWOPD distills CodeV-SVA-14B into a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct student. The student has the highest reported pass@1, pass@5, and pass@10 on NL2SVA-Human and NL2SVA-Machine among the compared models, including specialized baselines and 671B general-purpose models.

papers.title: Is Agentic AI Ready for Real-World Hardware Engineering? A Deep Dive with Phoenix-bench
papers.summary: We ask whether agentic AI systems built for software engineering transfer to realistic hardware engineering. Existing hardware LLM benchmarks isolate sub-tasks but none jointly requires repository navigation, hierarchy-aware localization, Electronic Design Automation (EDA) executable verification, and maintenance-style patching. We introduce \textbf{Phoenix-bench}, a synchronized corpus of 511 verified Verilator instances from 114 GitHub repositories, each shipped with the developer patch, design-flow labels, fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass testbenches, and a Docker-pinned EDA environment so resolved-rate differences reflect agent behavior rather than toolchain availability. Using Phoenix-bench we run a uniform evaluation of four commercial agents and eight open-source agentic structures across four LLM backbones, plus two diagnostic interventions (file-level oracle localization and one round of testbench-log feedback). Three findings emerge. (i)~Software and hardware are fundamentally different engineering tasks: the same agent loses 37\% to 58\% from SWE-bench Verified to Phoenix-bench because hardware bugs propagate across parallel instantiated modules through signal flow rather than along a software-style call graph, and software-tuned agents stop at the symptom file instead of tracing back through the instantiation chain. (ii)~Failures concentrate on design control-flow / finite state machine (FSM) bugs, verification testbench bugs, and hard cases that demand cross-hierarchy signal-flow tracking and coordinated multi-file edits. (iii)~Localization granularity matters far more than localization itself: a perfect file-level oracle yields only $+1.4$\% because the agent then breaks files that did not need editing, while a single round of test case feedback lifts resolved rate by $42$\% to $45$\% because the test case tells \emph{where} the bug is and \emph{what} the fix has to look like.

papers.title: Specifying Hardware Communication as Programs
papers.summary: To test and debug hardware modules, it is common to write two programs. A driver maps high-level transactions to cycle-level I/O behavior, and a monitor looks at the low-level I/O trace and recovers transactions. Both programs bridge the same abstraction gap between RTL and functional models. Writing them separately risks inconsistency. ProtoLang is a DSL for specifying hardware protocols. The same ProtoLang program can both drive and monitor transactions. Users specify RTL communication protocols as succinct imperative programs. We present a novel reconstructor algorithm that, given a ProtoLang specification and a waveform, automatically infers a transaction-level trace consistent with the waveform. We demonstrate ProtoLang's utility via case studies focusing on the Wishbone and AXI-Stream interconnects, showing that ProtoLang can model complex protocol features such as burst mode. We highlight how our tools can identify protocol violation bugs in real-world implementations.

papers.title: Semi-asynchronous Federated Learning in Flower: Framework Extension and Performance Assessment
papers.summary: This paper presents an extension of the Flower federated learning framework to support Semi-Asynchronous Federated Learning. The proposed approach adapts the traditional synchronous paradigm to better handle client heterogeneity and straggler effects. By introducing a semi-asynchronous training strategy, the system allows partial synchronization among clients while maintaining training efficiency and scalability. We implement and evaluate the proposed modification within Flower, instantiated as the FedSaSync strategy, demonstrating improved robustness and reduced idle time compared to fully synchronous baselines in heterogeneous environments. The results show that SAFL can balance convergence stability and system efficiency in heterogeneous environments typical of edge and distributed learning scenarios.

papers.title: BrownoutMoE: Learning Structure-Aware Expert Grouping for Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts Model Serving
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models (LLMs) are increasingly served on multi-GPU clusters in cloud data centers, where inference must stay accurate and responsive under bursty demand. Expert access in MoE inference is highly imbalanced: a few hot experts process most tokens, whereas many cold experts fragment kernels and leave GPU parallelism underused. Existing serving systems optimize runtime execution but keep the original expert organization. We propose BrownoutMoE, a structure-aware serving framework inspired by the brownout paradigm in cloud computing. It learns layer-wise expert grouping offline with reinforcement learning, using the post-distillation error as the reward. Grouping-consistent distillation trains one united expert per group, and an online controller adjusts how often united experts replace cold experts under latency objectives. On eight A100 GPUs, BrownoutMoE reduces accuracy degradation by up to 71.4% relative to index-order grouping, improves unfused throughput by up to 2.24x over vLLM, and lowers saturated decode latency by 38%.

papers.title: Flex: A Foundational Proof-Producing Horn Solver
papers.summary: Constrained Horn Clauses (CHCs) are a versatile intermediate representation for program verification, but leading CHC solvers rely on SMT-based reasoning over supported background theories. Specifications involving user-defined recursive functions or bespoke operators can require additional semantic encodings and reasoning beyond these theories. We observe that CHCs are existentially quantified propositions in a foundational logic, and so can be proved within an interactive theorem prover, where specifications can use native definitions, and users can complete proofs when automation stalls. However, in a foundational setting, every Horn variable solution must be justified by a kernel-checked proof. We present Flex, a proof-producing CHC solver implemented as a Lean metaprogram, that combines predicate synthesis with proof construction. Flex comprises a suite of tactics: Zap, which synthesizes strongest predicates for acyclic Horn variables and exploits their structure to construct elimination proofs without any proof search; Fix, which uses predicate abstraction over templates built from arbitrary Lean terms, discovered by scraping the CHCs and associated definitions, to infer inductive invariants for cyclic Horn variables; and a certifying pipeline that keeps external SMT-based solvers like Spacer and Eldarica outside the trusted computing base. We use Flex to verify the functional correctness of sorting algorithms, hash tables, ring buffers from the Tock OS kernel, and Rust std library challenges. We show that Zap constructs elimination proofs 28.2x and 44.6x faster than grind and aesop, respectively. With Zap and Fix, Flex automatically proves 98.0% of the refinement-typechecker CHCs in our evaluation.

papers.title: ETAS: An Effect-Typed Language for Agent Systems
papers.summary: Agent systems are programs that coordinate language-model queries, tool calls, human approvals, and ordinary computation, yet existing frameworks wire them together as opaque library objects outside compiler analysis. Treating agent systems from a programming-language perspective, we present Etas, an effect-typed language that elevates agents, tools, workflows, and behavioral specifications to first-class, compiler-checked constructs. Crucially, Etas separates escaping effects from persistent effect request summaries: handlers change how an operation is interpreted without erasing its effect request from the summary, while trace specs constrain permitted effect requests and their order. The compiler composes effect request summaries across calls and handlers, discharging satisfied trace specs statically and keeping a residual monitor where dynamic paths remain uncertain. We formalize Core Etas with terminal handlers, a trace-spec monitor construction, and an abstract analysis over monitor states, proving preservation, progress, effect coverage, and trace-spec safety. We implement a compiler, an optimizer, and a checked interpreter using Rust. Across compiler fixtures and coding-agent scenarios written in Etas, Etas successfully enforces callable bounds, effect operation ordering, and handled effect request visibility with zero mismatches. The compiler also implements agent-specific optimizations that reduce execution time by 23.2%. Across 12 Etas workflows, the combined token optimization passes reduce input tokens by 67.8% on paired-correct executions. First-class agent abstractions also enable recursive self-evolution for Etas programs. Across five harness evolution iterations, task accuracy rises from 69.9% to 78.9%.

papers.title: Formal Verification of an Out-of-Order Multiprocessor against an In-Order Weak-Memory ISA
papers.summary: Out-of-order multiprocessors are critical components of modern hardware, and their verification is desirable as they are difficult to correct once shipped. Existing literature simplifies and improves instruction set architectures (ISAs) for such processors, but they assume the processor correctly implements the ISA rather than proving it. We present the first formal verification of an out-of-order multiprocessor $\text{Core}_{\text{Impl}}$ against an in-order, weak-memory RISC-V ISA, RISC-V$_{\text{prom}}$. Our central component is $\text{Core}_{\text{InO}}$, an in-order one-instruction at a time core specification, enabling us to confine out-of-order reasoning to a single core. We decompose the main proof into two refinements. The core refinement proves that $\text{Core}_{\text{InO}}$ is a correct specification for $\text{Core}_{\text{Impl}}$. The system refinement shows that RISC-V$_{\text{prom}}$ is a correct specification for multiple $\text{Core}_{\text{InO}}$ connected with shared memory, leveraging the simplicity of $\text{Core}_{\text{InO}}$ in the proof. All of our proofs are mechanized in Rocq, with large language model agents heavily used to automate proof writing. We synthesized $\text{Core}_{\text{Impl}}$ into the Bluespec hardware description language, and validated it produces the intended weak behaviors and adheres to the official RISC-V test suite.

papers.title: High-Level Synthesis of Efficient Pipelines with Visibility Control
papers.summary: High-level synthesis (HLS) raises the abstraction of hardware design from concurrent register-transfer level (RTL). Among the forms of parallelism HLS exploits, pipelining demands fine-grained control over pipeline structure and hazard resolution to achieve competitive power, performance, and area (PPA). However, existing tools either lack such control or sacrifice sequential semantics to provide it. We present an HLS tool that embeds fine-grained pipeline control in a sequential programming model while generating synchronization logic only where needed to resolve the pipeline's potential hazards. The tool builds on visibility control, a novel programming abstraction that unifies hazard resolution techniques including stalling, bypassing, speculation, deferred commit, and register renaming. We evaluate on in-order RISC-V cores, histograms, and an AES accelerator. On RISC-V cores, we implement stall, bypass, speculation, and register renaming; on histograms, we implement scheduling strategies that previously required RTL or concurrent programming models. Compiled pipelines outperform HLS tools with sequential semantics and achieve PPA comparable to hand-written RTL.

papers.title: DrainSinkhorn: Instance-Resident Batched Entropic Optimal Transport on GPUs
papers.summary: Many learning pipelines call entropic optimal transport (OT) inside a loop, and each call is a batch of small, independent problems: one per image in detection label assignment, per patch pair in point-cloud registration, per frame pair in tracking, and per tile in domain decomposition. General GPU solvers launch every Sinkhorn update over the whole batch and run the batch until its slowest problem stops, so practitioners write a kernel for each shape or drop OT. We present DrainSinkhorn, a batched Sinkhorn solver that makes each problem of the batch, an instance, the unit of GPU execution. Wherever an instance fits on chip, one GPU thread block solves it from start to finish and exits as soon as the instance converges, freeing its slot for a pending instance. With a fixed iteration count, several instances share a thread block, and the forward map and its exact gradient take one launch each. Larger instances leave later launches once they converge. On tracking and domain-decomposition workloads, DrainSinkhorn is 2.73-10.75x faster than OTT-JAX, the fastest general batched GPU solver in our comparison, and 5.3-34x faster than POT. The gain is largest on calls with thousands of instances. In training layers it is 1.05-2.8x faster than OTT-JAX and 9.9-24x faster than the Sinkhorn modules of OTA and GeoTransformer, cutting label assignment from 16.3% to 4.7% of each GPU's training step and making GeoTransformer's patch matching 10.4x faster in a training step.

papers.title: CARA: Exact Local Repair Queries for Cloud Consolidation
papers.summary: Cloud consolidation evaluates alternative workload placements to reduce overload under fixed host and migration budgets. A controller repeatedly queries the same demand history, but consumes only a small ranked result and one final repair. Shared aggregation and incremental assignment reuse individual computations but still reconstruct constraints and numerical certificates for many related queries. This preparation can erase the savings from skipping exact profiles. We present CARA, which compiles seed-universal movement constraints and family-wide load-error budgets, then acquires exact profiles according to certified ranking keys. The compiler leaves a migration-bounded assignment core and preserves ranked records, physical mappings and continuation state; a separate admission stage evaluates one frozen repair. On all 12,006 hourly series from four workload sources, CARA executes controlled queries 4.75 times faster than compact complete profiling and heterogeneous packed queries 3.05 times faster than family-local execution; across 300 budgeted consolidation decisions, it reduces excess over FFD by 35.8% and attains the lowest excess among the compared policies.

papers.title: eIRWR: Enhanced Iterative Random Walk with Restart for Scalable Root Cause Analysis in Microservices
papers.summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) in microservice systems must find the faulty service behind symptoms that spread across hundreds or thousands of dependent services. Graph-based random walk methods propagate anomaly evidence over the service dependency graph. However, existing anomaly-restart walks restart from the raw anomaly vector, which is often dominated by strongly anomalous downstream victims rather than the less anomalous source. Through a controlled ablation of a basic anomaly-restart walk, the Iterative Random Walk with Restart (IRWR), we show that its ``resilience damping'' is equivalent to a higher restart probability in Personalized PageRank (PPR). Basic IRWR is therefore no stronger than a restart-tuned PPR, which we adopt as a fairer baseline. We then present Enhanced IRWR (eIRWR), which goes beyond restart tuning. It (a)~concentrates restart mass on the most suspicious nodes through power-law sharpening and (b)~adds self-loops and backward edges so that probability accumulates at cascade sources. On three large topologies (12K--25K nodes) from the Alibaba Microservice Trace Dataset, eIRWR is the most accurate of the compared graph-based methods at every level of root-cause visibility. At visibility $v = 0.3$, it reaches a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of $0.78$, about four times a restart-tuned PPR and nine times the best other baseline. At high visibility, it reaches MRR\,$= 0.95$ and runs in under 30\,ms on graphs with 17K nodes, so it is suitable for online use.

papers.title: Claude Code Complete User Handbook
papers.summary: Claude Code is an agentic work environment: a language model operating in a loop with filesystem access, shell execution, browser control, scheduled and cloud execution, external tool connections through the Model Context Protocol, and multi-agent orchestration. Its capability envelope now exceeds what one practitioner can supervise by attention alone, and its failure modes are systemic rather than local: an unreviewed hook, an over-scoped connector, a stale completion condition, an autonomous routine inheriting every credential on an account. This book is a task-oriented reference for operating that system safely and productively, written for practitioners accountable for the result. It advances four propositions. First, capability without a defined and observable completion condition is not productivity. Second, instruction, permission enforcement, sandboxing and operating-system isolation are four distinct layers of a control stack, the first advisory and the other three enforced, and conflating them is the most common cause of loss of control. Third, third-party skills, plugins, marketplaces, channels and MCP servers are software supply-chain dependencies and must be governed as such. Fourth, the correct unit of trust in agentic work is observed evidence, not an agent's closing statement. Thirty-four chapters run from installation to a fully verified capstone, with a governance part on managed policy, data residency and retention, observability and accessibility. Every product claim carries a citation to a primary source; an evidence ledger records where a claim in circulation was found wrong, what a later re-verification changed, and what remains unverified. Controls are mapped to seventeen external frameworks in a crosswalk, and an organisational adoption maturity model is proposed. Claims not confirmable from primary sources are labelled UNVERIFIED rather than softened.

papers.title: Comparison of Algebraic Block Multi-Coloring and Leiden Methods for Parallel Preconditioning in the ICCG Method
papers.summary: In the application of incomplete Cholesky preconditioning to the incomplete Cholesky-conjugate gradient (ICCG) method, forward and backward substitutions exhibit sequential dependencies that constitute a major bottleneck for parallelization in multicore environments. To alleviate this bottleneck, the algebraic block multi-coloring (ABMC) method achieves both parallelism and data locality through block-wise coloring. However, ABMC requires the number of blocks to be specified as an input parameter in advance. This study evaluates the Leiden method as an alternative blocking approach for parallel preconditioning in the ICCG method. As a community detection technique that maximizes a quality function for graph partitioning, the Leiden method automatically generates blocks that reflect the matrix structure without requiring the number of blocks a priori. We partition the adjacency graphs of sparse matrices using the Leiden method and utilize the resulting blocks for parallel preconditioning. We implement the Leiden method using modularity and the constant Potts model as quality functions and compare its performance with that of the ABMC method in terms of the number of iterations, execution time, and L2 cache efficiency across eight symmetric positive definite matrices. The experimental results demonstrate that the Leiden method with the constant Potts model achieves performance comparable to that of the ABMC method configured with an optimized number of blocks.

papers.title: Carbon-aware Resource Management for Latency-Sensitive Cloud Computing Environments: A Taxonomy and Future Directions
papers.summary: The proliferation of cloud-based latency-sensitive workloads, such as autonomous driving, real-time healthcare services, industrial automation, immersive interactive services, and intelligent AI-based applications requires infrastructures tuned to meet stringent latency constraints. Today, these workloads are reshaping the cloud from a general-purpose computing platform into a diverse ecosystem of workload-specific cloud environments. As demand for latency-sensitive workloads grows, cloud providers must scale their infrastructures accordingly, adversely increasing the carbon footprint and challenging net-zero goals. However, the strict performance requirements and rigid deployment patterns used to satisfy latency Service Level Objectives (SLOs) constrains conventional carbon optimization. Therefore, novel carbon-aware techniques are needed to exploit application-specific opportunities for reducing both operational and embodied carbon footprints while preserving latency guarantees. This survey examines carbon-aware resource management for latency-sensitive cloud computing environments. We introduce a holistic taxonomy that organizes existing techniques by carbon management objective, workload management mechanism, control architecture, system tier, latency requirements, and deployment stage. Then, we use this taxonomy to classify and critically analyze existing approaches, revealing the interactions and trade-offs between latency guarantees and operational and embodied carbon reduction. Finally, we identify limitations in the literature and present a structured research agenda for the design of sustainable latency-sensitive cloud systems.

papers.title: Seamless Reconfiguration for DAG-BFT (Technical Report)
papers.summary: Byzantine Atomic Broadcast in Asynchronous networks has been studied extensively for decades. In a fully asynchronous system with even one possible crash failure, the FLP impossibility result rules out deterministic consensus, motivating randomized protocols that achieve termination with probability one. More recently, DAG-Rider popularized a new abstraction in which processes continuously reliably broadcast blocks to construct a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and then locally derive a total order using a randomized perfect coin. This separation of dissemination from ordering has renewed interest in asynchronous DAG-based Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) and inspired numerous protocols that improve expected latency or throughput. Reconfiguration, however, remains largely unexplored. Existing DAG-based BFT protocols generally assume a static set of processes, whereas deployed systems must occasionally add or remove nodes in response to operational demands. Existing solutions are not seamless; they either pause the system or delay membership changes until a predetermined epoch boundary. This may be impractical and can introduce downtime. A single agreed switching round is difficult to use seamlessly: by the time processes learn it, the dissemination layer may already have advanced beyond it. In this work, we present a seamless reconfiguration protocol for Asynchronous DAG-based Byzantine Atomic Broadcast. Our protocol allows the DAG to continue growing while the membership and corresponding quorum thresholds change, without halting the system. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first protocol to provide seamless reconfiguration for DAG-based Byzantine atomic broadcast in a fully asynchronous network.

papers.title: Cartesian Byte-Bank Models and Warp Lag Screening for GPU Lossless Compression
papers.summary: Headerless multi-channel 16-bit streams degrade unit-lag differencing, byte shuffling, and chunked GPU codecs when adjacent words belong to distinct sensors. On even-length 16-bit tiles (<= 16 MiB), GPX6 pairs a 32-lane CUDA warp lag screen with a threshold-free 3 x 2 Cartesian conditional byte-bank range Asymmetric Numeral Systems (rANS) coder and OpenMP Zstandard-1 framing. Across 30 subject-disjoint waveform files (88.90 MB, N = 27 subjects), GPX6 compresses to 26,449,754 B (29.75% aggregate; 42.68% subject mean; 40.74% six-cohort mean across 338.25 MB) at 424.1/279.0 MB/s host-to-host on RTX 4080 Laptop GPU and 266.9/166.4 MB/s on A100-80GB, reaching 474.1/482.3 MB/s (4.81/5.98 GB/s resident) on 30-tile A100 batches. Completing GPX4 into GPX6 saves +2.59 pp subject mean, localized to step-quantized BIDMC telemetry (+6.24 pp vs. +0.20 pp on smooth cohorts). Under 1-payload screening, GPX6 saves +10.59 pp ([+8.09, +13.28] pp) over faster zero-order GPU nvCOMP ANS, beats 16-bit MANS and 64 KiB nvCOMP Zstd (2.17x-2.49x faster encode), and maps CPU, audio, and 2D boundaries.

papers.title: Tutorial on Closed-Loop and Application-Aware Digital Twins for Future Wireless Networks
papers.summary: To support emerging applications such as extended reality, autonomous systems, and large-scale cyber-physical infrastructures, next-generation wireless networks must evolve beyond traditional communication paradigms toward tightly integrated and closed-loop systems. Digital Twin Networks (DTNs) have recently emerged as a key enabler of this transformation by bridging the physical and digital worlds through real-time, bidirectional interactions and adaptive control mechanisms. In this tutorial, we provide a comprehensive overview of DTN design and optimization across multiple system dimensions. Specifically, we first introduce the fundamental design principles of DTN creation, including high-fidelity twin modeling, telemetry integration, and cyber-physical synchronization. We then present resource optimization and semantic-driven DTNs, where application-aware objectives and semantic abstractions guide efficient data processing, communication, and decision-making. Subsequently, we explore physical-layer optimization techniques for DTNs, emphasizing joint sensing, communication, and adaptive wireless resource control. Furthermore, we examine DTN-guided network management and feedback optimization, focusing on closed-loop learning, real-time control, and reinforcement-driven adaptation between digital twins and physical networks. Finally, we review ongoing standardization efforts and enabling tools that support the practical deployment of DTNs in real-world systems. This tutorial aims to provide a unified perspective on DTNs as an emerging paradigm for application-aware, AI-native, and closed-loop wireless systems, and to highlight key challenges and future research directions in this rapidly evolving field.

papers.title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Collaborative edge large language model (LLM) systems often require repeated prefill computation when task contexts are transferred between agents. Reusing previously computed key--value (KV) caches can eliminate this overhead, but requires KV-cache delivery before the receiving agent begins decoding. Under strict deadlines and unreliable edge links, complete KV cache transfer may be infeasible, making the timely delivery of useful KV information critical. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that combines prioritized source transmission with adaptive loss recovery. PriorityFEC first organizes KV blocks into a utility-aware source queue to prioritize important information. It then employs ACK-sliding Streaming FEC and a lightweight Double Deep Q-Network (Double-DQN) scheduler to dynamically balance source delivery and repair transmission under deadline constraints. We implement PriorityFEC in a distributed edge LLM-serving prototype and evaluate it using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple workloads. Experimental results demonstrate that PriorityFEC preserves more useful KV information and achieves substantially higher task accuracy than competing transport schemes, particularly when the deadline is insufficient to deliver the complete KV cache.

papers.title: Who Plans, Who Edits? Verified, Cost-Aware Division of Labor for LLM-Driven Analog Layout Repair
papers.summary: Language-model agents can repair analog layouts when sign-off tools check every edit, but which model should plan a repair, which should edit it, and at what cost remain open questions. In our tool-grounded repair agent, models only choose bounded layout operators; sign-off tools rerun each task's contract checks after every edit, so failing layouts are never accepted. On layout-versus-schematic (LVS), design-rule checking (DRC), and post-layout repairs of three designs (a production high-voltage digital-to-analog converter (DAC), a 5-V oscillator, and a SKY130 operational transconductance amplifier (OTA)) with six tier-matched models from two vendors, 182 blind runs show that cheap models execute plans but rarely succeed alone (the cheapest model: 1 of 11 runs alone, 16 of 17 under a flagship planner; p < 0.001), cheap planners fail more often, and no fixed assignment is cheapest on every task. We propose a learning controller that selects models for each role and the escalation order from the first tool evaluation and updates Bayesian estimates after every attempt. With rules and initial estimates frozen before testing, the controller fixed 7 of 8 episodes on four sealed held-out tasks, matching the OpenAI flagship alone, at 15-40% of the flagship's spend per fix on three tasks but 8% higher spend overall. The cheapest mid-tier model alone fixed 6 of 8 at the lowest overall spend per fix but missed the hardest task. All 32 extracted DAC repairs match the human-guided LVS repair's integral nonlinearity (INL) within 0.005 least significant bits (LSB) at every code.

papers.title: Matching Workloads to Blackwell: Power-Resolved Benchmarking of NVIDIA B200 and B300 across HPC and AI Workloads
papers.summary: We evaluate NVIDIA B200 and B300 (Blackwell Ultra) GPUs on two independent eight-GPU clusters, spanning computer-vision inference and training, LLM inference with Llama-3-8B and 70B~\cite{llama3}, and six production HPC codes. The B300 is not a uniform successor to the B200: it trails by up to 5.6$\times$ on convolutional inference, 8$\times$ on 3D vision transformer training, 24--27\% on 70B LLM throughput, and 16$\times$ on double-precision Quantum ESPRESSO. We resolve the convolutional deficit using per-GPU board power rather than throughput alone: on the affected workloads the B300 draws only 36--53\% of its 1100\,W envelope, whereas on ViT-Large, which it wins, both parts saturate at 95--97\% of TDP. Because our harness keeps inputs resident in device memory, a host-side data pipeline is excluded by construction, localizing the cause to per-kernel cost. Two B300 nodes of identical silicon differ by 2.1$\times$ in time-to-first-token solely from a development vLLM build. We give per-workload procurement guidance.

papers.title: High-Throughput Private Information Retrieval with on-CPU Accelerators
papers.summary: We present AltoPIR, the first PIR system that exploits the capability of emerging on-CPU matrix accelerators such as Intel AMX. Unlike existing solutions, AltoPIR achieves high-performance PIR through efficient batching without requiring discrete accelerators. However, the on-CPU accelerator has only a few small registers and shares its core with request handling. As a result, it runs far below its peak rate while its operands arrive from memory, and it remains idle while its core handles requests. To keep the accelerator busy, we design mechanisms that reduce both the memory traffic of a batch and the core cycles spent on each request. Our experimental results show that AltoPIR outperforms existing CPU-based solutions by up to 50.1x.

papers.title: Exploring the Power Consumption of ERC-4337 Bundling on Server Infrastructure
papers.summary: The Ethereum ecosystem offers the most widespread support for Decentralised Applications (DApps), with over 120 networks currently documented as using variants of the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) for core execution logic. The ERC-4337 standard provides convenient access to DApps for users who do not possess the required cryptocurrency or prefer flexible authorisation of DApp actions. The infrastructure for ERC-4337 implementation can be deployed on any EVM network. However, to aggregate user requests and submit them to the EVM network, ERC-4337 requires operating a bundler, an additional component. Recently, the potential use of ERC-4337 was boosted by another standard, EIP-7702, which can enable ERC-4337 utility for any existing user account. However, the use of the combined EIP-7702/ERC-4337 pattern remains considerably low at less than 6% of EIP-7702 activity. We believe that this underutilisation is at least partly caused by the low number of existing bundling services and their popularity, currently fewer than 15 publicly documented. Expanding the number of bundler nodes would benefit the ecosystem but would introduce operational costs, part of which is represented by the added nodes' power consumption. In this paper, we provide a thorough view of the bundling power consumption aspect using server-grade infrastructure, evaluating both CPU and RAM consumption, as well as the overhead of container-based deployments specific to production environments.

papers.title: GSPIM: A Temporal-Locality-Aware 4D Gaussian Splatting Accelerator with Polymorphic PIM and Multi-Frame Rendering Dataflow
papers.summary: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) enables high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis for dynamic scenes, supporting free-viewpoint video, mobile XR, and autonomous systems at the edge. Methods using explicit 4D distributions, keyframe interpolation, or anchor binding share two GPU data-movement bottlenecks. Temporal filtering follows model record loading, wasting LPDDR5 bandwidth on inactive data. Frame-isolated execution also overlooks highly overlapping active sets and depth relationships across adjacent frames, reloading shared attributes when working sets exceed on-chip cache capacity. To address these bottlenecks, we present GSPIM, a temporal-locality-aware 4DGS accelerator for PIM-enabled edge devices. Polymorphic PIM adapts a shared near-memory datapath to representation-specific field layouts and selection procedures. It filters and compacts valid data into contiguous inputs before the GPU accesses complete attributes, reducing ineffective transfers. Multi-Frame Rendering Dataflow reuses active attributes and stable depth relationships within a temporal window, reducing repeated work across frames. Hybrid Dataflow Scheduling overlaps near-memory data preparation with GPU rendering to reduce waiting. Evaluation combines a GPU-PIM model calibrated to Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB with a 1z DRAM physical implementation of the added circuits. Across three 4DGS methods and six dynamic scenes, GSPIM achieves a 4.15x geometric-mean speedup and a 4.99x geometric-mean energy-efficiency improvement over a fully optimized frame-by-frame GPU baseline. The maximum scene-level PSNR difference is 0.011 dB, and the added physical footprint is 18.7172 square millimeters across 32 LPDDR5 dies.

papers.title: Performance Portability of Out-of-Kernel Optimizations on GPUs: A Molecular Docking Case Study
papers.summary: Achieving performance portability is challenging for irregular scientific applications built as repeated multi-kernel GPU pipelines, because throughput depends on out-of-kernel decisions as much as on kernel efficiency. Using molecular docking as a representative case study, we propose an out-of-kernel tuning methodology that treats batching policy, worker concurrency, and per-worker memory allocation as explicit optimization parameters, replacing backend-dependent occupancy-driven choices with a more portable execution strategy based on explicit resource bounds. We implement this methodology in the muDock mini-app under a manager/worker execution model where multiple host workers share a GPU through independent streams. We then evaluate the methodology on NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs across CUDA, HIP, and SYCL implementations. Across all evaluated platform/backend pairs, the memory-bounded formulation exceeds the peak throughput of the occupancy-guided baseline. The fully tuned methodology improves the end-to-end throughput on all tested configurations, achieving an average speedup of 1.53x over the baseline.

papers.title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-based Management of Continuum Resources
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path. This study argues for a different use of LLMs: a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent or declared context change, above a fast, deterministic tactical controller that handles all low-latency runtime actions. We formulate intent compilation as a continual instruction tuning problem, because management intents arrive sequentially and accumulate while infrastructure and workload contexts drift. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. On a continuum simulator with a 2B backbone and parameter-efficient adapters, preliminary results show that naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, that replay of stored examples nearly prevents this forgetting, and that the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/lilanpei/continuum-intent-compiler.

papers.title: Augur: An Online Learning-based Hardware Data Prefetcher using Reservoir Computing
papers.summary: Machine-learning-based hardware prefetchers can learn complex access patterns, but practical deployment demands online adaptation, low-latency inference, and modest hardware cost. We present Augur, a hardware delta prefetcher based on next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC) that meets all three requirements. Augur formulates delta prediction as a history-based regression problem. It constructs a fixed-size reservoir from hashed delta features over a short context window and predicts the next delta using a single dot product. The model is updated online via one-step SGD and requires no offline pre-training, no per-benchmark tuning, and no floating-point arithmetic. Replacing the integer multiplications traditionally used to generate nonlinear reservoir features with bitwise AND operations removes all feature-generation multipliers with no loss in performance. Because Augur regresses a continuous delta, it needs no action set chosen offline for a fixed set of workloads. Augur pairs the reservoir with a simple Markov-based delta predictor for simple delta patterns, and with a selective issuance policy that filters and throttles wasteful prefetches; this policy accounts for about 40% of Augur's advantage and also improves Pythia. Evaluated on 169 traces spanning GAP, Ligra, PARSEC, SPEC CPU 2006, SPEC CPU 2017, and AI workloads, Augur outperforms the state-of-the-art ML-based delta prefetcher by 2.9%, 4.5%, and 5.3% in geomean speedup on 1-, 4-, and 8-core systems, respectively, while achieving ~2x higher prefetch accuracy and 37.8 percentage points fewer overpredictions. Augur is practical to implement at 33 KB storage, 0.32 sq. mm area, and 32.7 mW in 12 nm.

papers.title: CU-3D: A Scalable Legality-Aware RTL-to-GDS Flow for 3D-IC Physical Design
papers.summary: Face-to-face (F2F) hybrid bonds shorten interdie connections, but data, clock, and power-grid (PG) connections must be realized together. CU-3D is a RTL-to-GDS physical design flow based on commercial EDA tools. It derives role-compatible hybrid-bond (HB) sites from a 17-metal ASAP7-based technology model, complete HB footprints, and constructed PG geometry. To coordinate partitioning with placement flexibility, Scaled refines an inherited 2D placement, whereas Fresh places the receiving die first and uses its pin locations and clock loads to guide placement of the other die. Data and clock HB assignments are jointly optimized while retaining alternative data sites and reserving capacity for subsequent PG assignment. The selected HB sites and stacks are preserved during 3D clock-tree synthesis, supply-aware cell insertion, and routing. Across eleven designs, including a 133-macro processor, the flow achieves zero backend DRC violations and passes signal-connectivity checks. Nine paired designs admit lower-footprint, lower-power implementations; four improve setup WNS. On JPEG, early joint planning gains 87 ps and mobility-aware partitioning gains 346 ps. Path analysis explains why cell-delay savings can outweigh net-delay increases.

papers.title: On Higher-Order Reachability Games vs May Reachability
papers.summary: We consider the reachability problem for higher-order functional programs and study the relationship between reachability games (i.e., the reachability problem for programs with angelic and demonic nondeterminism) and may-reachability (i.e., the reachability problem for programs with only angelic nondeterminism). We show that reachability games for order-n programs can be reduced to may-reachability for order-(n+1) programs, and vice versa. We formalize the reductions by using higher-order fixpoint logic and prove their correctness. We also discuss applications of the reductions to higher-order program verification.

papers.title: ExclaveFL: Verifiable Claims for Federated Learning using Exclaves
papers.summary: In federated learning (FL), data providers jointly train a machine learning model without sharing training data. This makes it challenging to provide verifiable claims about the trained model, e.g., related to the employed training data, data sanitization, or training algorithm---a malicious data provider can simply deviate from the correct training protocol without detection. Prior FL training systems have used trusted execution environments (TEEs) to protect the training computation, relying on the confidentiality and integrity of TEEs. TEE confidentiality, however, has been shown to be vulnerable to various attacks, e.g., via side channels. We describe ExclaveFL, a system for training FL models that establishes verifiable claims about models through fine-grained runtime attestation proofs. Since such proofs only require integrity, ExclaveFL generates them using exclaves, which are integrity-only execution environments without software-managed secrets, making them immune to data leakage attacks. ExclaveFL uses exclaves to attest data transformations during FL training, and the runtime attestation proofs then form an attested dataflow graph of the entire training computation. The graph is checked by an auditor to ensure that the trained model satisfies claims, e.g., about the use of data sanitization by data providers or aggregation by the model provider. Since exclaves require minor yet proprietary firmware changes, we evaluate a variant with similar performance but slightly weaker security guarantees on existing AMD SEV-SNP hardware. We show that ExclaveFL introduces less than 12% overhead compared to unprotected FL model training.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Techniques for Distributed Entanglement Generation and Purification
papers.summary: We develop a purification-aware optimization framework for distributing high-fidelity entangled states over quantum networks. In repeater-based architectures, the framework jointly selects entanglement swapping, fusion or graph-state growth, and purification operations to maximize generation rate under a fidelity threshold. Different purification models can be incorporated through their fidelity-update, success-probability, and latency rules. We introduce purification-augmented generation trees and dynamic programming (DP) algorithms for entangled-pair (EP) distribution. Hypergraph-flow linear programming (LP) formulations support level-based structures and concurrent generation across multiple trees and demands. We extend the framework to GHZ states and arbitrary graph states constructed from remote EP resources, introduce graph-state construction primitives, and derive closed-form fidelity-vector updates for GHZ fusion and purification and graph-state growth and purification. We provide optimal formulations under the adopted models, discretization, and purification bounds, together with efficient DP and LP heuristics. We bound fidelity- and rate-discretization errors and establish convergence for fixed constructions under stated regularity conditions. NetSquid simulations of EP generation using our LP approach show an average 160% increase in generation rate over the compared prior approaches, with gains up to 330% in some scenarios. GHZ and graph-state simulations demonstrate the heuristics' effectiveness in balancing generation rate, output fidelity, and computational overhead.

papers.title: CrypTorch: Unified PyTorch-based Auto-tuning Compiler for Private Machine Learning Inference
papers.summary: MPC-based ML uses secure multi-party computation (MPC) to execute machine learning (ML) workloads across multiple parties without requiring any party to reveal its private data or model parameters. Our characterization study finds that the performance of state-of-the-art MPC frameworks is often dominated by operator-approximation strategies, where ML operators not natively supported by MPC are replaced with iterative methods or polynomials. These approximations are typically chosen heuristically by each framework and applied globally. As a result, they can be unnecessarily expensive in some cases, yet insufficiently accurate in others. We find that the best approximation choice depends on the context, target framework, and application, making a single globally fixed approximation fundamentally suboptimal. To address this problem, we design CrypTorch, a multi-stage compiler for MPC-based ML that supports multiple MPC frameworks as backends. At the core of CrypTorch is its auto-tuning stage, which extracts cost estimates from the target MPC backend and quality estimates from a proxy PyTorch execution, and uses them to automatically select a set of approximations that maximizes performance while satisfying the given quality constraint. We show that CrypTorch's auto-tuner improves performance across multiple MPC backends by 1.14--1.60x without degrading accuracy, and by 1.17--1.92x with less than 3% accuracy degradation. CrypTorch's unified design also improves programmability and usability by allowing multiple backends to share other common compiler functionality and optimizations. We further show that the auto-tuner extends to a related fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) backend, reducing the number of bootstrapping operations by 1.31--1.65x.

papers.title: Mind the Gap: Cross-RFC Formal Analysis Exposes DNSSEC's Hidden Vulnerabilities
papers.summary: This paper presents a cross-RFC formal analysis of selected DNSSEC mechanisms using SAPIC+ models of cryptographic operations and stateful caching. We analyze properties concerning data origin authenticity, integrity, chain of trust, and authenticated denial of existence within these models. Our analysis shows that core authentication properties hold under the modeled assumptions, while wildcard expansion, the mechanism that bridges positive and negative authentication, exhibits a cross-RFC interaction vulnerability that defeats DNSSEC's integrity guarantee. Specifically, we discover Cross-Zone Wildcard Cache Poisoning: a new attack in which a malicious zone operator exploits a gap in the DNSSEC specifications to poison resolver caches with forged records for some domains outside its authority, served to clients as DNSSEC-authentic. The tested versions of all four major resolvers implementing the affected caching optimization accept the malformed wildcard material. The resulting impact depends on the resolver's synthesis path. All four vendors have publicly released fixes. The distinctive integrity failure is a synthesized, attacker-chosen positive answer with the Authenticated Data (AD) bit set: prior attacks instead exhausted availability, downgraded to AD=0, or skipped validation. Our models also identify two cross-RFC availability flaws and rediscover three known attack classes. We test six resolvers and measure deployment prerequisites through focused resolver and TLD scans. We propose updates to four RFCs.

papers.title: DateSAT: A Framework for Solving Date and Period Constraints
papers.summary: Dates and calendar periods (i.e., days, months, years) appear frequently in tasks involving analysis of software, data, and documents. Prior research has shown that computer logic involving dates and calendrical calculations is error-prone due to tricky rules (e.g., irregularly sized months), ambiguities (e.g., scheduling one month from "January 31st"), and edge cases (e.g., leap years). However, existing program analysis and verification tools do not provide native support for dates, making it hard to reason symbolically about calendrical arithmetic. This paper presents DateSAT, the first framework for expressing and solving satisfiability constraints involving dates and calendar periods. The paper first formalizes an input language and the semantics of date and period arithmetic. The paper then presents four strategies for solving DateSAT constraints based on reductions to SMT formulas involving integers, with mechanized proofs of their correctness, and an implementation of each using Z3 as a backend. We curate a dataset of 800 DateSAT constraints synthesized using LLM prompting, grammar-based sampling, and mining legal documents, and present an empirical evaluation of DateSAT solver performance, which shows that the encodings have complementary strengths and that routing each constraint to a suitable encoding solves more constraints than any single encoding.

papers.title: Validating direct solvers for Newton's gravitational N-body problem, and the systematic comparison between IEEE floating point and Posits
papers.summary: We present a systematic comparison between arbitrary precise arithmetic and integration, IEEE-754 compliant floating point arithmetic (fp16, bfp16, fp32, double precision fp64, and quadruple precision fp128), and two implementations of Posits (type III unum) for solving Newton's chaotic N-body problem. Each implementation is benchmarked with arbitrary precise calculations to objectively evaluate their performance in precision as well as speed. We rely on hardware and compiler implementations for fp64, and software implementations for arbitrary-precision arithmetic and Posits. Half precision arithmetic (fp16, bfp16, and Posits$<16,1>$) are insufficiently precise for solving Newton's equations of motion. Single precision (fp32, and Posits$<32,2>$) could be used for statistical ensemble calculations, but lead to relatively large errors in any individual strong encounter. All 64-bit implementations fp64 as well as Posits (Posits$<64,3>$) experience difficulty in our tests. One of the implementations of Posits (Universal) gives precision comparable to fp64 but is slow (by at least an orders of magnitude compared to fp64 after correcting for the more efficient hardware support for the latter). The other (CPPPosits) has a speed comparable to fp64 but has systematically larger errors (by about an order of magnitude compared to fp64 with excesses exceeding two orders of magnitude). As a consequence, this implementation leads to a systematic drift in the result space and has difficulty resolving close encounters. Posits and fp64 have difficulty when integrating a dynamical system in a moving reference frame; testing Galileo invariancy. In their current implementation, Posits do not seem to be the ideal alternative for fp64 when integrating chaotic or stiff ordinary differential equations, such as Newton's equations of motion.

papers.title: LLM-Driven Algorithm Design for Quantum Circuit Synthesis based on Binary Decision Diagrams
papers.summary: Quantum circuits are central to implementing quantum algorithms on quantum devices, where quantum gates must be reversible. Many quantum algorithms rely on Boolean functions, which must therefore be implemented reversibly within quantum circuits. Reversible circuit synthesis provides a way to translate such Boolean functions into reversible circuits. Binary decision diagrams (BDDs) offer a scalable approach to this task, but the resulting BDDs and circuits depend heavily on variable ordering. Existing ordering heuristics commonly minimize BDD size because it is closely tied to the circuit size. However, BDD size is an imperfect proxy for the quantum cost of the synthesized circuit (QCC). We propose \texttt{QuantumEvo}, an evolutionary framework that uses an LLM as a heuristic generator for QCC-aware BDD variable ordering. Instead of predicting orderings directly, \texttt{QuantumEvo} searches over ordering heuristics initialized from multiple heuristic families. Candidate heuristics directly manipulate variable orderings using standard BDD operations and are selected by downstream QCC. The discovered heuristic, HGA-QE, modifies the sifting step inside a genetic algorithm so that the procedure is better aligned with QCC. Across the benchmark set, HGA-QE achieves a 70.9\% tie-or-win rate against the per-function best baseline and is strictly best on 13.5\% of the functions. The results demonstrate broadly competitive QCC performance, with HGA-QE showing a clearer relative advantage in strict wins on the two benchmark suites drawn from sources different from the data used for heuristic discovery.

papers.title: HELENA for 5G NR LEO NTN Channel Estimation: A Comparative Evaluation
papers.summary: Deep Learning (DL)-based channel estimation has shown high accuracy and low latency in terrestrial 5G NR, but Low Earth Orbit (LEO) Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTNs) introduce Doppler and synchronization impairments that may require NTN-specific architectures. We investigate whether HELENA, a dual-attention neural channel estimator originally designed for terrestrial channels, remains effective after NTN retraining and suitable across high-performance and power-constrained inference platforms. Its unchanged architecture is trained on paired receiver-compensated and residual-impaired datasets and evaluated alongside terrestrial-origin, NTN-specific, and classical estimators. HELENA's SNR-averaged Normalized Mean Squared Error (NMSE), computed by arithmetic averaging in linear scale, remains within 0.29 and 0.72 dB of the most accurate learned estimator, AttRNet, in the two conditions, respectively. It outperforms global Linear Minimum Mean Squared Error (LMMSE) under compensation and all evaluated LMMSE variants under residual impairments, although profile-aware filtering achieves lower error under compensation. On an RTX PRO 4500, FP16 TensorRT inference reaches 0.0573 ms 99th-Percentile (P99) latency, below the adopted 0.5 ms estimator budget. On a 10 W Jetson Orin NX, HELENA consumes 66.0% less energy per sample than AttRNet, but its 0.9620 ms P99 exceeds the budget; only the less accurate LSiDNN-48 meets it. Thus, HELENA remains effective without NTN-specific redesign for the evaluated task, while accurate embedded inference remains a latency challenge.

papers.title: When Tool Calls Succeed but Workflows Fail: Anomalies at the Agent-Tool Boundary
papers.summary: AI agents increasingly execute long-running workflows that externalize effects through independently supplied tools. Under retries, speculative execution, concurrency, and partial failures, the resulting external state may be inconsistent with the workflow's intended resolution: required effects may be missing or duplicated, aborted effects may survive, and committed effects may depend on provisional state that is later withdrawn. Advanced transaction models address related failures, but assume that lower-level operations expose the semantics they depend on: whether an effect occurred, whether it can be compensated, staged, or safely reordered. Shared agent-tool interfaces usually do not. We contribute an effect-history model that separates events in the external world from the runtime's observations of them, and a catalog of eight recurring external-effect anomalies. From the catalog we derive the boundary capabilities required to exclude each anomaly in general, and four points where black-box tool invocation alone cannot provide a general guarantee. We then ask how much of this is expressible in a widely used shared tool interface, measuring the use of the standard annotation vocabulary across 98,291 tools exposed by reachable remote servers in the official Model Context Protocol (MCP) registry. The fields are widely emitted but provide only coarse call-level hints, and none of the required capabilities is fully expressible. These results motivate reusable transactional contracts at the tool boundary.

papers.title: TileBench: A Controlled Benchmark for Performance Evaluation and Bottleneck Diagnosis of Tile-Based Programming Models
papers.summary: Tile-based programming models, such as Triton and cuTile, aim to simplify high-performance kernel development, but their practical performance, tuning behavior, and usability remain difficult to compare systematically. We present TileBench, a controlled benchmark for evaluating Triton and cuTile on NVIDIA B200 GPUs under matched operator semantics and comparable implementation structures. TileBench contains 45 operators covering diverse AI-kernel patterns and memory/computation behaviors. Each task provides a PyTorch reference, verified Triton and cuTile implementations, standardized data-types (dtype) and input-size sweeps, default and autotuned configurations, roofline-based metrics, and profiling-guided diagnosis. Our evaluation shows that performance gaps are workload-dependent: cuTile excels on a small cluster of Tensor-Core/TMA-friendly kernels, while Triton is stronger on many irregular, streaming, and bandwidth-bound operators. We further evaluate LLM-generated cuTile and Triton kernels and find that Triton is consistently more token-efficient than cuTile under the same iterative refinement protocol. TileBench is publicly available at https://github.com/Deep-Learning-Profiling-Tools/Tilebench.

papers.title: Self-organizing recruitment cascades couple Levy search to a clustered maximum-entropy resource field
papers.summary: Foraging recruitment is modeled as a contagion: an agent finding a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade on the group's communication network. Because activation is degree-normalized, crowding shuts the cascade off, causing the swarm to aggregate on a resource and then disperse to explore again. Acting on the cascade moves agents in space, rewiring the network; recruitment and exploration are thus one coupled process, and removing this coupling alone abolishes self-limitation. Recruitment spreads only within a connectivity window bounded below by percolation onset and above by degree-blocking. The swarm self-organizes to the near-critical edge of this window--self-organized quasi-criticality--hovering near but below the critical point without settling onto a size-invariant critical state, with a finite-correlation-time activity spectrum (Lorentzian-like, not 1/f) consistent with local criticality. Recruitment raises harvest up to 2.7x over solitary search on sparse, clustered fields and loses (down to 0.37x) on abundant or uniform ones; because resources generically aggregate, the favourable regime is the common one. The Levy search and resource field are both least-committal: a maximum-caliber walk coupled to a maximum-entropy point process whose generic sign is clustered, with the optimal search exponent tracking the field's fractal dimension. Heavy-tailed Levy exploration crosses sparse voids while recruitment cascades exploit clusters by switching agents to short local steps, binding exploration and recruitment into a single self-organizing cycle.

papers.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
papers.summary: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which Gemini 4 agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 2.57x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 12x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

papers.title: RBLA+: Efficient Rank-Specific LoRA Adapter Extraction for Federated Fine-Tuning with Heterogeneous Clients
papers.summary: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client's rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model. Two common approaches to rank-specific extraction are direct rank truncation and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the dense update. Direct prefix truncation keeps the leading columns of one aggregated factor and the corresponding rows of the other. It is cheap but can increase reconstruction error. The dense SVD approach first forms the product of aggregated LoRA factors. It then decomposes this matrix and retains the leading singular components to construct adapters at the target rank. This gives the optimal rank-constrained approximation in Frobenius norm but incurs significant computational overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose RBLA+ as an extension of RBLA. It uses established compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update. It also accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Across vision and language tasks, RBLA+ improves accuracy over RBLA in multiple heterogeneous settings. In CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters, RBLA+ has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline. RBLA+ preserves each client's prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.

papers.title: LoCoJAX: Host-Local Coordination for Small-Model RL on TPUs
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly targets small language models, and executing these workloads efficiently across multiple accelerators requires effective coordination. On TPUs, Pathways-based RL uses a single controller to coordinate computation across hosts. This execution model is effective for large models, but its coordination computational costs are harder to amortize when small models repeatedly invoke short computations. To characterize these computational costs, we sweep dense models from 0.6B to 405B parameters on TPU v7x under a decode-heavy workload and measure how host and network computational overhead vary with model size. At 0.6B, host orchestration occupies 36% of step time and network communication 2%, whereas for large models, estimated network computational costs dominate the non-compute time. Motivated by these findings, we present Local Coordination JAX (LoCoJAX), which implements local rollout and reward processing on each TPU host with synchronous global training. In controlled comparisons against a tuned and optimized Pathways baseline on Qwen3-0.6B across three workloads and 8-64 TPU v7x chips, its colocated mode (LoCoJAX-CO) is 1.3-3.6x faster per step; on GSM8K, it completes a step faster on 8 chips than Pathways does on 64. Finally, a Ray-managed disaggregated mode (LoCoJAX-DA) overlaps rollout and training on separate hosts, and placement experiments establish when this overlap compensates for dividing devices and transferring weights: only when rollout dominates the step and receives most of the hosts. On NuminaMath-CoT at 256 chips, giving rollout 75% of hosts cuts step time by about 15% compared with LoCoJAX-CO.
